newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean president to detail policies on Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean president to detail policies on Tuesday.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam will unveil policies on Tuesday to deal with wildcat strikes that threaten to wreak havoc in the country's slowing economy, presidential aides said on Monday.
Public attention is riveted on Kim after an umbrella union group vowed to stage a bruising battle with the government unless the president repealed a new labour law.
"The president will cover all important issues at a New Year news conference tomorrow, including the economy, the strikes, North Korea and security issues," one aide said.

Kim has so far been largely silent on the labour issue and even retreated to a hot spring resort as industrial action flared following unilateral passage of a new labour bill in parliament by his ruling party on December 26.
"The labour issue will be the most critical factor in our economy this year," said Sakong Eun-duk, senior economist at the private Hanwha Economic Research Institute.
"Industrial unrest, if not checked quickly, will deal a huge blow to exports and the overall economy," he said. "The profitability of local companies has already plunged."

The central bank has said the country is set to post a record current account deficit of more than $22 billion, four times the original forecast of $5-6 billion, for 1996 when economic growth dropped sharply to an estimated 6.9 percent from 9.0 percent in 1995.
The deficit in trade in goods and services would represent more than 4.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), the total of goods and services produced by the country.
Economists say deficits repeatedly amounting to more than five percent of GDP would be dangerous for any economy.
The government says economic woes stem from high-cost, low-productivity manufacturing and argues that a new labour law is needed to help address the structural problem.

Strikes swept South Korea since the ruling party, in a clandestine six-minute National Assembly session, railroaded through the new labour bill allowing employers to lay off workers, eroding decades of near-total job security.

Almost 150,000 workers, including some 100,000 at the giant Daewoo and Hyundai groups, walked out on Monday when state prosecutors summoned about 20 leaders of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions for questioning.
Confederation president Kwon Young-kil vowed to ignore the prosecution order and threatened to intensify protests unless President Kim announced a repeal of the new law on Tuesday.
Byun Hae-ryong, a director of the Korea Employers' Federation, said strikes cost employers 340 billion won ($403 million) in lost production between December 26 and January 3.
Share prices plunged on the Seoul bourse on Monday with the composite stock index closing more than two percent lower.

Sakong said the strike would deter companies from investing in a year when investor sentiment was dampened by a presidential election due in December and threats posed by uncertainty over North Korea.
"A fall in investment would spell lacklustre production in the future and that will in turn cut back jobs," he said.

President Kim is expected to discuss the cautious steps the Seoul government is considering to promote detente with North Korea, which last week apologised for a submarine incurion into the South in September.
